newsitem.title: USA: U.S. broiler production seen rising in 97, 98-USDA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. broiler production seen rising in 97, 98-USDA.

text.p: U.S. broiler production will increase about six percent in 1997 and likely rise strongly again in 1998, U.S. Agriculture Department livestock analyst James Nix said in a speech prepared for delivery at USDA's annual Agricultural Outlook Forum.
"It is hard to argue against a continued upward movement in broiler production during the next several years," Nix said in the speech, which will be delivered Tuesday.
He said the increase in output in 1999 probably would slow from 1998's rise but said another drop in beef output "should make it a relatively favorable year for broiler producers."

The livestock analyst said U.S. broiler exports are projected to increase in 1997 and long-term prospects point to continued gains. In 1996, exports were up 16 percent from the prior year and nearly 300 percent above the 1990 level.
He said high levels of exports to Russia should continue in the next few years and that strong growth in demand in Hong Kong and China was expected to support further export gains.
Nix said growing demand worldwide for broiler meat should support the anticipated growth in total U.S. broiler exports.
On prices, Nix said the 1997 annual average was expected to dip about one cent from 1996's level of 61.2 cents per pound.
"Broiler prices in 1998 and 1999 likely will slip from the 1997 level as broilers find their niche between falling beef supplies and rising pork output," he said in the speech.

Nix said the forecasts were the product of USDA's Meat Animals and Poultry Interagency Commodity Estimates Committees and might differ from those in USDA's Baseline forecasts because they were based on newer data.
